name: Ormond
lede: Ormond is a light, greyish brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, dated by the dictionary itself to 1920, and one of the more common named colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A trade name from 1920
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places this color at plate 14, chip A4, and dates its own first record to 1920, a decade before the dictionary itself was published [1]. The ISCC-NBS system did not coin a separate name; it only cites the same chip when classifying the color as a light grayish brown [1]. Where the name "Ormond" comes from is not documented in the sources we checked, undocumented here [1].

In our color graph its closest named relatives are [[broccoli-brown]], almost the same, and [[taupe]] and [[folkstone]], both close behind [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of Ormond covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 2,115 works, more common than 93 per cent of our named colors [3]. The painter most devoted to it is Francisco Bayeu, in 5 of his 13 works here, about 3.3 times his museums' baseline [3]. It most often shares a canvas with [[plain-mouse]] and [[biscuit]], at 5.2 and 4.5 times the expected rate [3]. The earliest dated appearance in our archive is the year 900, a millennium before the name's own 1920 record, a look-alike hue, not proof of pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
